claims.claim: Metaphysics can be described as the field of philosophy concerned with identifying what is real and with questions about being, self, causation, free will, and related matters.
Metaphysical realism holds that the objects, properties, and relations in the world exist and have their nature independently of how inquiring agents think about them.
Challenges to metaphysical realism include questions about how beliefs and language represent a mind-independent world and whether the categories in an inventory of reality are concept-dependent.
An illusion involves a present object appearing other than it is, while a hallucination is an object-like experience without an object of the relevant kind being perceived.

The possibility of illusion and hallucination creates a philosophical problem about the relation between perceptual experience and the world, but those possibilities are not by themselves a demonstration that no external world exists.

Global skepticism requires an argument that inability to rule out a skeptical hypothesis defeats justification for an ordinary claim; merely describing a possible error does not supply that whole argument.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether the world has a fully mind-independent structure and whether human representations can capture it without unresolved conceptual or semantic problems.
positions: Metaphysical realism treats the world's objects, properties, and relations as mind-independent.
Anti-realist challenges dispute or qualify that independence and raise representation and conceptual-scheme problems.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson defines the central disagreement, distinguishes it from ordinary confidence, and avoids claiming a final resolution.
